[00:00:00.452] The next set of operators we will look at are your Boolean or logical operators. In Boolean algebra, we have a collection of Boolean operators which are denoted by AND, OR, and NOT.

[00:01:02.628] So when you see the column for the AND operator, you can see that it only results in true when both the values of X and Y are true. So we can conclude.
[00:01:17.744] that the and operator returns true if both values are true and false otherwise.
[00:01:24.548] Whereas the OR operator returns false only if both the values are false. So even if one of the operings are true, it will always return a true value.
[00:01:39.140] And the not operator always gives you the inverse of the value of the variable. So if x were false, it would return true, and if x were true, it would return false. Let's look at this with some examples.

[00:02:33.188] Unary operators will always precede the operate. So not true will give you false and not false will give you true. Now what I'm going to do is use

[00:03:16.612] Now, in your Boolean expression, there are true and false equivalent values. We know that true and false denote the Boolean values, but there are other false values as well.
[00:03:30.788] A zero number is a false value, an empty string or empty collections are treated as false values as well.
[00:03:40.804] And true values are any non-zero numbers, any non-empty string, and any non-empty collections apart from the keyword tree. So let's go back to the idle platform.
[00:03:56.548] So instead of giving the Boolean values true and false, why is it giving me an empty string or a zero as a result? This is because of the concept of short circuit evaluation. Now the logical operant.

[00:05:26.852] But you can see here, it doesn't give me an error, but works just fine. The reason being, since this evaluates to a true equivalent value, and the next operator is an OR operator.
[00:05:40.864] It knows that the result is always going to be true, so it returns the value that denotes a true value or a true result. Therefore, it doesn't evaluate the second operant at all.
